Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper is an exposition of the so-called injective Morita contexts (in which the connecting bimodule morphisms are injective) and Morita $\alpha$contexts (in which the connecting bimodules enjoy some local projectivity in the sense of Zimmermann-Huisgen). Motivated by situations in which only one trace ideal is in action, or the compatibility between the bimodule morphisms is not needed, we introduce the notions of Morita semi-contexts and Morita data, and investigate them. Injective Morita data will be used (with the help of static and adstatic modules) to establish equivalences between some intersecting subcategories related to subcategories of modules that are localized or colocalized by trace ideals of a Morita datum. We end up with applications of Morita $\alpha$-contexts to $\ast$-modules and injective right wide Morita contexts.

Since there are settings in which just one trace ideal is relevant, or where no compatibility condition between the bimodule maps is required, the paper defines and examines the concepts of Morita semi-contexts and Morita data. Using injective Morita data, together with static and adstatic modules, the work proves equivalences among certain overlapping subcategories associated with module classes that are localized or colocalized through the trace ideals arising from a Morita datum. The paper develops and organizes several generalizations of classical Morita theory, focusing on situations in which the usual strict compatibility or surjectivity assumptions are weakened.

It first studies **injective Morita contexts**. In a classical Morita context, two rings are connected by bimodules together with bimodule morphisms satisfying certain compatibility conditions. In the injective version considered in the paper, the connecting bimodule morphisms are assumed to be **injective**. This allows the authors to analyze Morita-type relationships in cases where the maps do not necessarily identify the relevant tensor products with the rings, but still embed them in a controlled way. The injectivity condition makes it possible to relate module categories through trace ideals and to study subcategories determined by these embeddings.

The paper then discusses **Morita α-contexts**. These are Morita contexts in which the connecting bimodules satisfy a form of **local projectivity** in the sense of Zimmermann-Huisgen. Local projectivity is weaker than finite generation and projectivity, but still strong enough to ensure useful duality and density properties. By imposing this condition, Morita α-contexts provide a flexible framework for extending Morita-theoretic results beyond the classical finitely generated projective setting. They are particularly useful for describing when certain functors behave well on subcategories of modules controlled by trace ideals.

To deal with more asymmetric or incomplete situations, the authors introduce the notions of **Morita semi-contexts** and **Morita data**. A Morita semi-context captures cases where only part of the usual Morita-context structure is available, for example when there is only one connecting morphism or only one relevant trace ideal. Morita data are even more general: they allow the study of pairs of bimodules and morphisms without requiring the full compatibility conditions between the bimodule maps. These concepts make it possible to formulate and prove Morita-type results in settings where the classical context is too restrictive.

A central role is played by **injective Morita data**. Using these data, the paper studies **static** and **adstatic** modules, which are modules naturally recovered from the adjunctions induced by the bimodules. Static modules are those for which the relevant counit map is an isomorphism, while adstatic modules are those for which the corresponding unit map is an isomorphism. The authors use these ideas to establish equivalences between certain intersecting subcategories of module categories. These subcategories are described in terms of localization or colocalization by trace ideals, and the injectivity assumptions ensure that the trace ideals control the equivalences in a precise way.

Finally, the paper gives applications of Morita α-contexts to two important settings. The first concerns **∗-modules**, where the local projectivity conditions allow the authors to connect the theory with module classes generated or cogenerated by a fixed module. The second concerns **injective right wide Morita contexts**, where the developed machinery yields equivalences and structural results for broader classes of Morita contexts than those covered by the classical theory. Overall, the paper shows that injective contexts, α-contexts, semi-contexts, and Morita data provide a unified framework for extending Morita theory to nonclassical and one-sided situations.

The paper investigates several generalizations of classical Morita theory, with particular emphasis on situations where the usual hypotheses of a Morita context are weakened. It begins by studying injective Morita contexts and Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts, and then introduces the notions of Morita semi-contexts and Morita data. These new frameworks are designed to treat cases in which only one of the trace ideals is available, or in which the usual compatibility conditions between the bimodule morphisms of a Morita context are not assumed.

A central theme of the paper is the use of injective Morita data to compare module categories through localization and colocalization techniques. In this setting, the authors consider suitable classes of modules, especially static and adstatic modules, and show that these classes provide the correct categorical framework for obtaining equivalences. More precisely, under appropriate injectivity assumptions, the paper establishes equivalences between localized or colocalized subcategories of module categories associated with the rings and bimodules appearing in the Morita data.

The work also clarifies the role of trace ideals in weakened Morita contexts. In classical Morita theory, two trace ideals and two compatible connecting morphisms are typically required. By introducing Morita semi-contexts, the paper is able to isolate and study one-sided versions of this structure. Morita data then provide a still more flexible setting, allowing the authors to work with pairs of bimodules and morphisms even when the full compatibility conditions of a Morita context are absent.

In addition, the paper applies the theory of Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts to the study of \(*\)-modules. This connects the abstract categorical results with module-theoretic conditions such as generation, cogeneration, and torsion-theoretic properties. The paper further examines injective right wide Morita contexts, showing how the developed machinery can be used to obtain equivalences and structural results in this broader setting.

Overall, the paper extends classical Morita theory by developing tools that work under weaker assumptions than those required for ordinary Morita contexts. Through the notions of Morita semi-contexts, Morita data, injective Morita data, and Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts, it provides a unified approach to equivalences between suitable subcategories of module categories, especially those defined by localization, colocalization, static modules, and adstatic modules.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematics paper about injective Morita contexts, Morita α-contexts, Morita semi-contexts, trace ideals, static/adstatic modules, and applications to *-modules and injective right wide Morita contexts.
counterfactuals.output:
We study several extensions of classical Morita theory centered on injectivity and trace-type conditions. Starting from Morita contexts and their one-sided variants, we introduce and analyze injective Morita contexts, Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts, and Morita semi-contexts, emphasizing the role of the associated trace ideals in controlling adjunctions, equivalences, and approximation properties. For a bimodule \(M\), we investigate the static and adstatic subcategories determined by the tensor–Hom adjunction, giving criteria for when these classes are closed under natural homological operations and when they yield equivalences between distinguished module subcategories.

The main results characterize injective Morita contexts in terms of exactness properties, trace ideals, and the behavior of static and adstatic modules. We show how Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts provide a flexible framework for transferring injectivity and cogeneration conditions across rings, while Morita semi-contexts capture one-sided phenomena arising from non-surjective connecting morphisms. These constructions lead to refined descriptions of trace ideals as obstructions to full Morita equivalence and as invariants governing relative equivalences.

As applications, we apply the developed theory to \(*\)-modules and to injective right wide Morita contexts. In the case of \(*\)-modules, the static/adstatic correspondence yields structural criteria for when such modules induce equivalences on naturally defined subcategories. For injective right wide Morita contexts, we obtain characterizations in terms of trace ideals and relative injectivity, extending classical Morita theorems to broader settings where only partial or one-sided context data are available. The results unify several known forms of relative Morita theory and provide new tools for studying module categories through trace, injectivity, and adjunction-theoretic methods.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main contributions of a research article introducing Morita semi-contexts and Morita data motivated by injective Morita contexts and Zimmermann-Huisgen local projectivity.
counterfactuals.output:
The article’s main contribution is to develop a framework that unifies and extends ideas from **injective Morita contexts** and **Zimmermann-Huisgen’s local projectivity**. Its key points can be summarized as follows:

- **Introduction of Morita semi-contexts.**  
  The paper defines a one-sided or “semi” version of a Morita context, retaining only part of the usual Morita-context structure. This allows one to study situations where only one connecting map or one side of the context is available.

- **Introduction of Morita data.**  
  It further generalizes semi-contexts into “Morita data,” a flexible package of rings, modules, pairings, and compatibility conditions designed to capture module-theoretic situations that do not fit into classical Morita theory.

- **Connection with injective Morita contexts.**  
  The framework is motivated by contexts in which the connecting maps are injective rather than surjective or isomorphisms. The paper shows how such injective Morita contexts can be treated systematically using the language of semi-contexts and Morita data.

- **Extension of local projectivity ideas.**  
  Zimmermann-Huisgen’s notion of local projectivity is used as a guiding principle. The article reformulates local projectivity-type conditions in terms of the new Morita-data language, thereby broadening the scope of where these conditions can be applied.

- **Functorial and categorical consequences.**  
  The paper studies the module categories associated with these structures and identifies when certain naturally arising functors are faithful, full, or yield equivalences between suitable subcategories.

- **Unification of several constructions.**  
  Classical Morita theory, injective Morita contexts, rational module theory, and local projectivity phenomena can all be viewed as special cases or consequences of the proposed framework.

- **Conceptual simplification.**  
  By isolating the essential data needed for these generalized Morita-type relationships, the article provides a more flexible language for studying module categories where ordinary Morita equivalence is too restrictive.

In short, the article generalizes Morita-theoretic methods by introducing **Morita semi-contexts** and **Morita data**, showing that they provide a natural setting for injective contexts, local projectivity, and related categorical equivalences.

counterfactuals.output: We develop a framework for injective Morita data in module categories and relate it to localization and colocalization determined by trace ideals. Given a bimodule setting with an injective cogenerator-like object, we analyze the associated adjoint functors and identify the module classes on which the unit and counit morphisms become isomorphisms, namely the static and adstatic modules. We show that these classes admit intrinsic descriptions in terms of trace ideals and their induced torsion-theoretic structures, yielding localized and colocalized subcategories of module categories. The main results establish equivalences between suitable full subcategories of modules determined by injective Morita contexts, extending classical Morita equivalence beyond progenerator hypotheses. **Abstract.**  
We study Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts associated with rings, bimodules, and connecting morphisms satisfying weakened Morita-type compatibility conditions. Particular attention is given to the case in which the connecting bimodule morphisms are injective, allowing the structure of the context to be analyzed through the induced trace ideals. We describe how these trace ideals control the extent to which the context approximates a classical Morita context and record consequences for annihilators, faithfulness, and ideal-theoretic decompositions of the underlying rings. The exposition emphasizes the role of the images of the connecting maps as canonical trace ideals and explains how injectivity permits one to transfer structural information between the bimodules and their coefficient rings.

As an application, we discuss wide Morita contexts, where the usual bimodule framework is enlarged to accommodate broader module-theoretic or ideal-theoretic situations. We show how Morita \(\alpha\)-contexts provide a natural language for organizing such data and how trace ideals yield effective criteria for comparing, restricting, and reconstructing wide contexts. The resulting perspective unifies several familiar features of classical Morita theory with more flexible settings in which equivalences are replaced by trace-controlled correspondences. This provides a conceptual framework for studying generalized Morita phenomena in nonunital, nonfaithful, or partially defined contexts.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a mathematical paper summary explaining how Morita semi-contexts and Morita data generalize Morita contexts when only one trace ideal is relevant or compatibility of bimodule morphisms is unnecessary.
counterfactuals.output:
## Summary: Morita Semi-Contexts and Morita Data as One-Sided and Weak Forms of Morita Contexts

Classical Morita theory studies when two rings or algebras \(A\) and \(B\) have equivalent module categories. A standard device for doing this is a **Morita context**

\[
(A,B,\, {}_A P_B,\, {}_B Q_A,\, \tau,\mu),
\]

where \(P\) and \(Q\) are bimodules and

\[
\tau : P\otimes_B Q \to A, 
\qquad 
\mu : Q\otimes_A P \to B
\]

are bimodule morphisms satisfying the compatibility identities

\[
\tau(p\otimes q)p' = p\,\mu(q\otimes p'),
\]

\[
q\,\tau(p\otimes q') = \mu(q\otimes p)q'.
\]

The images

\[
\operatorname{Im}(\tau)\subseteq A,
\qquad
\operatorname{Im}(\mu)\subseteq B
\]

are the two **trace ideals** associated with the context. In the strongest case, when these trace ideals are all of \(A\) and \(B\), the context gives a Morita equivalence between \(A\) and \(B\).

The notions of **Morita semi-contexts** and **Morita data** weaken this classical structure in two different ways. They are useful when the full symmetry of a Morita context is not needed.

---

# 1. Classical Morita Contexts

A Morita context consists of the following data:

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\tau,\mu),
\]

where:

- \(A\) and \(B\) are rings, algebras, or more generally objects in a suitable monoidal category;
- \(P\) is an \(A\)-\(B\)-bimodule;
- \(Q\) is a \(B\)-\(A\)-bimodule;
- \(\tau : P\otimes_B Q \to A\) is an \(A\)-bimodule morphism;
- \(\mu : Q\otimes_A P \to B\) is a \(B\)-bimodule morphism.

The two maps must satisfy compatibility conditions ensuring that the two possible ways of multiplying expressions involving \(P\), \(Q\), \(A\), and \(B\) agree.

These compatibility conditions are essential if one wants to build a linking ring

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
A & P \\
Q & B
\end{pmatrix}
\]

with multiplication determined by \(\tau\) and \(\mu\). They also ensure that the functors

\[
P\otimes_B - : B\text{-Mod}\to A\text{-Mod},
\]

\[
Q\otimes_A - : A\text{-Mod}\to B\text{-Mod}
\]

interact coherently.

The trace ideals

\[
T_A=\operatorname{Im}(\tau)\subseteq A,
\qquad
T_B=\operatorname{Im}(\mu)\subseteq B
\]

measure how much of \(A\) and \(B\) is seen by the bimodules \(P\) and \(Q\). If both trace ideals are the whole rings, one obtains the usual Morita equivalence situation.

---

# 2. Morita Semi-Contexts

A **Morita semi-context** keeps only one side of the classical Morita context.

For example, a left-sided Morita semi-context may consist of

\[
(A,B,\, {}_A P_B,\, {}_B Q_A,\, \tau),
\]

where

\[
\tau : P\otimes_B Q \to A
\]

is an \(A\)-bimodule morphism.

There is no requirement that there also be a map

\[
\mu : Q\otimes_A P \to B.
\]

Thus only one trace ideal is available:

\[
T_A=\operatorname{Im}(\tau)\subseteq A.
\]

Similarly, one may have a right-sided semi-context

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\mu),
\]

with only

\[
\mu : Q\otimes_A P\to B
\]

and trace ideal

\[
T_B=\operatorname{Im}(\mu)\subseteq B.
\]

## Why Semi-Contexts Are Useful

Morita semi-contexts are appropriate when only one of the two trace ideals is relevant.

For example, one may only care about how \(P\) and \(Q\) generate an ideal of \(A\), without needing a corresponding ideal in \(B\). This happens in settings where one studies:

- one-sided equivalences;
- localizations;
- idempotent ideals;
- firm modules;
- rings with local units;
- categories generated by a single class of objects;
- partial Morita equivalences;
- trace ideals arising from a single adjunction.

In such situations, requiring the second map \(\mu\) and the full Morita compatibility conditions would impose unnecessary structure.

Thus a Morita semi-context can be viewed as a **one-sided Morita context**.

It captures the part of Morita theory governed by a single pairing

\[
P\otimes_B Q\to A
\]

or

\[
Q\otimes_A P\to B.
\]

---

# 3. Morita Data

Morita data are a different weakening of classical Morita contexts.

A Morita context requires two pairings

\[
\tau : P\otimes_B Q\to A,
\qquad
\mu : Q\otimes_A P\to B
\]

together with compatibility identities. By contrast, **Morita data** may consist of the same underlying bimodules and the same two morphisms, but without requiring the two compatibility relations.

Thus a typical Morita datum is

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\tau,\mu),
\]

where

\[
\tau : P\otimes_B Q\to A
\]

and

\[
\mu : Q\otimes_A P\to B
\]

are bimodule morphisms, but the conditions

\[
\tau(p\otimes q)p' = p\,\mu(q\otimes p')
\]

and

\[
q\,\tau(p\otimes q') = \mu(q\otimes p)q'
\]

are not imposed.

In this sense, Morita data generalize Morita contexts by separating the existence of the two pairings from their mutual compatibility.

## Why Morita Data Are Useful

Morita data are useful when both trace ideals are present,

\[
T_A=\operatorname{Im}(\tau)\subseteq A,
\qquad
T_B=\operatorname{Im}(\mu)\subseteq B,
\]

but one does not need the maps to define a genuine Morita context.

This may occur when one wants to study the two trace ideals independently, or when the maps arise naturally from different constructions and need not satisfy associativity-type relations.

Thus Morita data provide a flexible language for situations where:

- two bimodule pairings exist;
- both trace ideals are meaningful;
- compatibility is too strong or irrelevant;
- the goal is not necessarily to construct a linking ring or a Morita equivalence.

---

# 4. Relationship Between the Three Notions

The three notions form a hierarchy.

## Morita Context

A Morita context has:

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\tau,\mu)
\]

with both pairings and compatibility identities.

It is the strongest structure.

## Morita Datum

A Morita datum has:

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\tau,\mu)
\]

with both pairings, but compatibility may fail or be ignored.

Thus every Morita context is a Morita datum, but not every Morita datum is a Morita context.

## Morita Semi-Context

A Morita semi-context has only one pairing, for example

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\tau)
\]

or

\[
(A,B,P,Q,\mu).
\]

It records only one trace ideal.

Thus a Morita semi-context is useful when one side of the Morita context is all that is needed.

---

# 5. Conceptual Interpretation

Classical Morita contexts are symmetric: they relate \(A\) and \(B\) using two bimodules and two mutually compatible pairings. This symmetry is natural when proving equivalences of module categories.

Morita semi-contexts and Morita data relax this symmetry.

A Morita semi-context keeps only one pairing:

\[
P\otimes_B Q\to A
\]

or

\[
Q\otimes_A P\to B.
\]

It is therefore suited to one-sided trace theory.

Morita data keep both pairings but discard compatibility. They are therefore suited to situations in which the two trace ideals exist but no full Morita structure is required.

In short:

\[
\text{Morita context}
=
\text{two compatible pairings},
\]

\[
\text{Morita datum}
=
\text{two possibly incompatible pairings},
\]

\[
\text{Morita semi-context}
=
\text{one pairing only}.
\]

---

# 6. Main Mathematical Point

The main idea is that the essential information needed in many applications is not always the full Morita context. Often, one only needs:

1. a single trace ideal, or  
2. two trace ideals without the compatibility identities.

Morita semi-contexts address the first case.

Morita data address the second case.

Therefore they generalize Morita contexts by weakening the amount of structure required.

They allow Morita-type methods to be used in broader settings where full Morita equivalence is unavailable or unnecessary.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
